title: LLM App Architecture
summary: The practical stack for shipping an LLM-powered feature, beyond a single API call.

slides.markdown:
A production LLM feature is rarely "call the API, show the text" — it's a small system with its own architecture: an orchestration layer, a data store for context, and application logic wrapping the model call on both sides.

- **Model API** — the LLM call itself, one piece of a larger pipeline.
- **Orchestration** — the code that chains calls, manages state, and enforces structure.
- **Vector DB** — retrieval context when the app needs grounding (see [RAG](retrieval-augmented-generation)).
- Streaming, caching, and latency budgets shape the whole design.

slides.subTitle: Model API, orchestration, vector DB, app logic
slides.markdown:
A typical LLM app layers four pieces: the **model API** (hosted LLM or self-hosted inference), an **orchestration layer** that decides which calls to make, in what order, with what context; a **vector DB** holding embedded documents when the app needs grounding; and ordinary **application logic** — auth, business rules, the UI — that wraps around all of it exactly like any other backend.

The LLM call is usually the smallest piece of code in the system and the largest source of latency, cost, and unpredictability — architecture exists to manage that asymmetry.

slides.subTitle: Chains — composing multiple LLM calls
slides.markdown:
A **chain** (or pipeline) composes several LLM calls, each doing one narrow job, instead of asking one call to do everything — one call extracts facts from a document, a second summarizes them, a third drafts a reply using both. Splitting usually improves reliability, since each call has a simpler, more checkable job.

The cost compounds: more calls means more total latency and more places a failure can occur — chaining is a tool for reliability and modularity, not a default reach (see the pitfall on this trade-off).

slides.subTitle: Structured output as the integration seam
slides.markdown:
The point where an LLM app stops being "a chatbot" and starts being "a system" is **structured output**: forcing the model's response into a schema (JSON mode, function calling) so the rest of the application can consume it directly, instead of parsing free-form prose with regex and hoping the format doesn't drift.

This is what lets an LLM populate a form field, trigger a downstream API call, or write a row to a database reliably — the schema is the contract between the probabilistic model and the deterministic rest of your system.

slides.subTitle: Streaming responses
slides.markdown:
LLMs generate one token at a time, and a full response can take several seconds — **streaming** sends each token to the client as it's produced instead of waiting for the entire response, so the user sees text appearing immediately instead of a blank spinner.

Total generation time doesn't change, but **perceived** latency drops sharply — the first token typically arrives within a few hundred milliseconds, which is what users actually notice. Streaming also lets the UI render partial structured output before the full response completes.

slides.subTitle: Caching LLM responses
slides.markdown:
Two caching strategies solve different problems: an **exact-match cache** stores the response for an identical prompt, returning it instantly if seen again — cheap and safe, but only helps if inputs literally repeat. A **semantic cache** embeds incoming queries and matches against previously-answered *similar* queries within a threshold, catching paraphrases ("reset my password" vs "I forgot my password") an exact-match cache would miss.

Semantic caching needs careful threshold tuning — too loose, and it returns a wrong cached answer for a query that only sounded similar.

slides.subTitle: Chaining too many calls compounds cost
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Splitting a task into more, smaller LLM calls is always more reliable."

**Why it's wrong:** each added call adds its own latency (often can't run in parallel, since later calls depend on earlier outputs) and its own independent chance of a bad output — five 95%-reliable calls chained sequentially compound to roughly 77% overall success, not 95%.

**Correct model:** chain calls only where each step genuinely needs to be separately checkable or gated on the previous result; a single well-structured prompt beats a chain on both latency and reliability where it can do the job.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a request's path through the stack
slides.markdown:
![Sequence diagram: request flowing through app logic, orchestration, vector DB, and the model API](assets/request-sequence.svg)

The request rarely goes straight to the model. App logic authenticates and validates it, orchestration decides whether retrieval is needed and assembles the prompt, the model API returns a stream of tokens, and the same path unwinds in reverse to render the response.

Every hop on this path adds latency budget you have to account for — the model call is usually the single biggest chunk, but retrieval and orchestration overhead are not free.

slides.sectionTitle: Agents: when orchestration decides its own next step
slides.subTitle: A step beyond a fixed chain
slides.markdown:
A fixed chain runs the same sequence of calls every time. An **agent** loop instead lets the model itself decide, at each step, which tool to call next based on what it's seen so far — search the web, query a database, call an API — looping until it decides it has enough to answer.

This buys flexibility for tasks whose steps can't be predicted in advance, at the cost of a new failure mode: an agent can loop unproductively, call the wrong tool, or never converge, so agent architectures need step limits, tool-call validation, and the same guardrails as any other production LLM path (see [Guardrails & Production Safety](guardrails-safety-production)).
